🐾 Here’s the story behind Matt’s payments work at **JP Morgan Chase**.

From **August 2009 to June 2012**, Matt served as Technology Delivery Lead for ACCESS Next Generation, the bank’s unified corporate banking portal. Its regional payment systems had different data models, client configurations, entitlement structures, and compliance requirements. Bottomline Technologies’ WebSeries platform provided the foundation, but the bank needed payment capabilities well beyond its out-of-box offering, under aggressive Wall Street delivery timelines.

Matt managed a blended team of **40+** **Accenture** and bank resources across Mumbai, Bangalore, and the US. He defined the onshore-offshore engagement model and spent **70 to 80%** of his time embedded at Bottomline’s Portsmouth offices, coordinating with bank stakeholders in Chicago and New York/New Jersey. He worked with Bottomline to determine where native platform capabilities ended and bespoke engineering was required.

He designed and delivered ACH, wire, FX/cross-border, and federal tax payment modules, including NACHA file validation, payment integrity verification through Message Authentication Codes, and payment-type-specific permissions. He also delivered the centralized gateway for message transformation, protocol translation, and payment routing across **12 countries**.

Alongside that engineering, Matt brought together enterprise architects, security specialists, regional compliance officers, Bottomline, and the development team. They translated jurisdiction-specific requirements into data visibility rules, access controls, and rollout decisions. His entitlement engine introduced bulk permission changes and role-based profiles, reducing administration from days to minutes. He also led legacy payment data migration, production validation, and critical incident response, including root-cause coordination and daily leadership calls.

ACCESS launched in **April 2011**, consolidating regional systems into a portal serving **135,000+ clients** across **180+ countries**. The migration completed without disruption to live payments. Regional launches proceeded without regulatory blockers, with compliance dashboards becoming standard operational tooling.

answer_md:
🐾 Here’s how Matt describes his leadership philosophy.

Matt leads with empathy, clarity, and purpose. Many engineering teams he inherited were “over-processed, under-trusted, waiting for permission instead of owning outcomes.” His focus was to remove those barriers: make intent explicit, build psychological safety so people could speak honestly, and push decisions to the people closest to the work.

At **Accenture’s** Cloud Innovation Center, that meant coaching teams to think clearly, not just execute tasks. He used transparency, direct feedback, and open communication, alongside automation, continuous delivery, and quality-first engineering practices. Across work that included leading a **150-person** center, teams achieved **4x delivery acceleration** once they embraced lean product and modern engineering practices.

His “permit to fail” learning environment addressed teams’ fear of blame directly. Matt organized non-punitive post-mortems, emphasized lessons rather than finger-pointing, and supported lean, low-stakes experiments. In product incubation, he set expectations that early prototypes and user tests would likely fail intentionally: teams were testing assumptions before committing to costly builds. They applied those learnings to subsequent sprints, preventing recurrence of identified failure patterns and reducing wasted engineering effort.

He also built balanced teams: Product + Engineering + Design together. Engineers, product managers, and UX architects shared accountability rather than working through hierarchical handoffs. Pair programming, collaborative coding, retrospectives, and real-time feedback helped those teams reduce project delays and achieve **zero-defect production code** across client engagements.

Matt’s stated non-negotiables include integrity and respect, outcomes rather than optics, and continuous learning. He walks away from opportunities where intensity is not balanced with respect for people, regardless of title.

answer_md:
🐾 Here’s a time Matt took accountability for a delivery failure.

Matt was the tech lead on a global platform modernization for a financial services client. The program was under delivery pressure, with offshore teams running test cycles across development, QA, UAT, and production environments. IAM controls, environment segregation, and downstream access configurations had been inherited from prior phases, along with documentation.

Matt’s responsibility was to ensure a safe environment setup. Instead, he relied on that documentation without confirming its accuracy. He assumed the IAM configuration and environment boundaries were correct, did not audit who could trigger downstream jobs or email processes, and did not verify whether production customer data had been masked or scrubbed. Compensating controls, such as data masking and email interception, were not in place.

An offshore tester accidentally triggered an email job in UAT. It sent communications containing unmasked production customer data to **thousands of real clients**.

Matt took accountability and led the team through root cause analysis and remediation. They worked collectively to understand what happened and implement corrective controls. The root causes were insufficient IAM checks, unclear environment boundaries, and production data that had not been scrubbed from downstream environments.

The client demanded that the tester be removed from the project. Matt described that as “a systemic failure that resulted in an individual consequence.” His stated lesson was that “assumptions are risks in disguise.” IAM validation, environment verification, PII scrubbing, and risk ownership became day-one leadership responsibilities in his delivery approach.

IAM controls, environment segregation, and downstream access configurations had been inherited from prior phases, along with documentation.

Matt’s responsibility was to ensure a safe environment setup. Instead, he relied on that documentation without confirming its accuracy. He assumed the IAM configuration and environment boundaries were correct, did not audit who could trigger downstream jobs or email processes, and did not verify whether production customer data had been masked or scrubbed. Compensating controls, such as data masking and email interception, were not in place.

An offshore tester accidentally triggered an email job in UAT. It sent communications containing unmasked production customer data to **thousands of real clients**.

Matt took accountability and led the team through root cause analysis and remediation. They worked collectively to understand what happened and implement corrective controls. The root causes were insufficient IAM checks, unclear environment boundaries, and production data that had not been scrubbed from downstream environments.

The client demanded that the tester be removed from the project. Matt described that as “a systemic failure that resulted in an individual consequence.” His stated lesson was that “assumptions are risks in disguise.” IAM validation, environment verification, PII scrubbing, and risk ownership became day-one leadership responsibilities in his delivery approach.
